item.title: Six Mocktails: Coconut, Citrus, a Not-a-Mule, and Three for the Beach
item.description:
Six no-alcohol drinks. The first three cover different ground — creamy/tropical, bright/citrus, ginger-forward. The second three (watermelon mojito, virgin paloma, mango chili-lime) were picked to travel: each adds just one new bottle to the cooler and reuses lime, mint, agave, and soda already on the list below, rather than needing its own dedicated shopping trip. No expertise assumed on my end either — these are straightforward builds, not bartending theory.

Tools and stock worth having on hand

  • Cocktail shaker (or any lidded jar/container that seals — a mason jar works)
  • Jigger or a set of measuring shot glasses (1 oz / 2 oz)
  • Citrus juicer or reamer — fresh juice matters a lot more than bottled here, especially for lime
  • Muddler (the back of a wooden spoon works in a pinch) — for mint
  • Fine strainer, if shaking anything with pulp or muddled mint
  • Copper mugs, if leaning into the mule presentation — not required, just traditional
  • Full-fat coconut milk (canned, not the carton beverage) and coconut water are different ingredients below — don’t swap one for the other
  • A bottle of good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger bite, well-carbonated) and a bottle of club soda or seltzer
  • Agave syrup (or 1:1 agave-and-water simple syrup) — shared by the citrus spritz, the paloma, and the mango chili-lime below
  • Coarse salt or Tajín, for rimming glasses — one small shaker covers the paloma and the mango chili-lime

Packing these for the 5-hour drive down

This is a drive to a beach house with its own kitchen and freezer, not a cooler-only day trip — so the plan is simpler than packing for a walk to the sand:

  • Ice and blending both happen on arrival, not in the car. No need to haul ice down — the house has a freezer, and the blender/muddler work is easiest done in an actual kitchen anyway.
  • Bring whole watermelons and mangoes, not pre-juiced bottles. Whole fruit travels fine at room temperature for 5 hours and blends better fresh at the house than juice that’s been sitting since before you left — this also skips worrying about fresh watermelon/mango juice oxidizing or losing flavor over the drive, which was a real concern for pre-blending, and isn’t one for whole fruit. Bottled watermelon juice or mango nectar are still fine fallbacks if you’d rather not deal with a whole watermelon at all.
  • Pre-mix the chili-lime salt in a small shaker or travel container (or just bring a bottle of Tajín) — no different whether you’re rimming a glass at home or at the beach house.
  • Cans of soda/ginger beer over open bottles — they hold carbonation better over a long drive and don’t go flat if the trip is bumpy.
  • Fresh lime, grapefruit, and blood orange juice travel fine for 5 hours if juiced ahead and kept in the car’s AC rather than a hot trunk; agave, salt, and canned coconut milk don’t need any special handling at all.

Coconut Colada

Creamy and tropical — the coconut mocktail to reach for over a piña colada. Full-fat canned coconut milk gives real body; coconut water alone comes out thin.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 2 oz full-fat coconut milk (canned, shaken well first)
  • 3 oz pineapple juice
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • Splash of club soda or sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: pineapple wedge or wheel, mint sprig

Method: Shake the coconut milk, pineapple juice, and lime juice hard with ice — the coconut milk wants the agitation to emulsify and get that piña-colada texture. Strain into a glass over fresh ice, top with a splash of soda, garnish.

Variation: swap the club soda for a splash of ginger beer if you want more spice against the coconut.

Source: Be Well Table — Pineapple Coconut Mocktail.

Blood Orange Citrus Spritz

Bright and a little tart — blood orange juice has more depth than regular orange juice, and the color is the best-looking drink of the three if blood oranges are in season (roughly winter into early spring in most US markets; regular orange juice works fine off-season, just less dramatic).

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz blood orange juice (fresh-squeezed if you can get blood oranges; bottled is fine otherwise)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 0.5 oz agave syrup or simple syrup, to taste
  • Sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: orange wheel or twist

Method: Combine the juice, lime, and agave in a glass over ice, stir, then top with sparkling water. No shaking needed — this one’s built, not mixed.

Source: One Lovely Life — Blood Orange Mocktail.

The Not-a-Mule

A Moscow mule’s whole appeal is ginger heat against lime and fizz — none of that depends on the vodka, so dropping it loses less than you’d think. This is the one worth serving in a copper mug if you own them; the cold-metal thing is real, not just presentation.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 4 oz good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger, well-carbonated — the quality of the ginger beer is the whole drink here)
  • 0.75–1 oz fresh lime juice
  • Splash of club soda, optional, for extra fizz if the ginger beer alone isn’t lively enough
  • Ice
  • Garnish: lime wheel, mint sprig

Method: Fill a copper mug (or any glass) most of the way with ice. Add lime juice, top with ginger beer, stir gently — stir, don’t shake, or the ginger beer goes flat. Top with a splash of club soda if you want more sparkle. Garnish and serve immediately.

Source: Yummy Mummy Kitchen — Virgin Moscow Mule, Whisk Affair — Virgin Moscow Mule.

Watermelon Mojito (beach house-ready)

Reuses the lime and mint already on the list, plus club soda you’re already packing for the Not-a-Mule. The only new item is a whole watermelon — bring the fruit itself and blend at the house, rather than pre-juicing for the drive.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz watermelon juice (blended fresh from the whole fruit and strained, or bottled if you’d rather skip the blender entirely)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 4–5 mint leaves
  • Club soda or sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Garnish: mint sprig, watermelon wedge

Method: At the house — cube the watermelon, blend, strain out the pulp if you want a cleaner drink. Muddle the mint gently in the bottom of a glass, add lime juice and watermelon juice, fill with ice, top with soda, stir once.

Source: The Merry Thought — Watermelon Mojito Mocktail, The Real Food Dietitians — Watermelon Mojito.

Virgin Paloma (beach house-ready)

Same lime juice and agave as the Blood Orange Citrus Spritz, same sparkling water as everything else on this page — the only new bottle is grapefruit juice.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz grapefruit juice (fresh-squeezed if you’re juicing at home the night before; bottled is fine)
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 0.5 oz agave syrup, to taste
  • Sparkling water, to top
  • Ice
  • Salt (or Tajín) for the rim
  • Garnish: lime or grapefruit wedge

Method: Rim a glass with lime juice and dip in salt or Tajín, combine grapefruit juice, lime juice, and agave over ice, top with sparkling water, stir.

Source: Sweets & Thank You — Virgin Paloma, Mingle Mocktails — Paloma Mocktail.

Mango Chili-Lime (beach house-ready)

Reuses the lime, mint, and salt/Tajín already on the list — a whole mango (or bottled mango nectar, if you’d rather skip peeling and pureeing one) is the one new thing to bring.

Ingredients (1 drink):

  • 3 oz mango puree (blended fresh from a whole mango) or mango nectar
  • 0.5 oz fresh lime juice
  • 3–4 mint leaves
  • Sparkling water or club soda, to top
  • Ice
  • Chili-lime salt (Tajín, or your own chili/salt/sugar mix) for the rim
  • Garnish: lime wedge, mint sprig

Method: Rim the glass with lime juice and chili-lime salt, same as the paloma. Muddle or tear the mint into the glass, add lime juice and mango puree, fill with ice, top with soda, stir.

Source: Aura Bora — Mango Chili Lime Mocktail, Whole30 — Mango-Chili-Lime Mocktail.

item.title: Converting a Threaded SodaStream/Drinkmate to a 5 lb CO2 Tank
item.description:
Swapping the tiny 14.5 oz cylinder that ships with a threaded (screw-in) SodaStream or Drinkmate for an external 5 lb tank — same carbonation, without buying $15–20 exchange cylinders every 60 liters.

This only applies to screw-in machines. The connection depends on the TR21-4 thread — the “blue label” screw-in cylinder standard shared by classic SodaStream machines and Drinkmate. SodaStream Terra and Art use a push-in quick-connect cylinder and are not compatible with this approach — they need a different adapter, if one exists at all. Confirm your machine actually screws the cylinder in before buying anything.

The core idea: no regulator

The stock 14.5 oz cylinder feeds the machine unregulated, at something like 850 psi (CO2 tank pressure is a function of temperature, not fill level, until the tank runs dry — so a “full” 5 lb tank and an almost-empty one both sit around the same pressure at a given room temperature). The machine’s own trigger valve is what meters gas into the bottle in short bursts; it’s designed for that pressure already.

That means the standard approach is a direct adapter hose — CGA320 (the tank’s valve standard) on one end, TR21-4 (the machine’s cylinder thread) on the other — with no separate pressure regulator in between. Adding a regulator dialed down to, say, 130 psi would just give weaker carbonation than stock, not a safety improvement; the machine already expects full cylinder pressure.

Parts

  • 5 lb aluminum CO2 cylinder, CGA320 valve. Aluminum over steel — lighter, won’t rust internally. Buy new, not refurbished, DOT-approved with a current hydro-test date (5 lb aluminum cylinders in the US are DOT-3AL, hydro-tested every 5 years; the date’s stamped on the collar and a gas supplier will check it before filling or exchanging). VEVOR and Beverage Elements both make commonly-recommended 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinders.
  • CGA320 → TR21-4 direct adapter hose, 36–60 in, braided stainless or reinforced food-grade hose, rated well above tank pressure (most listings claim 4500–5000+ psi, which is the hose/fitting rating, not an indication you need that much pressure). Get one with a gauge and bleed valve — the bleed valve lets you depressurize the line before disconnecting, which matters (see below). Grab spare nylon washers/o-rings while you’re at it.
  • Tank strap or wall bracket. A pressurized 5 lb cylinder becomes a genuine projectile hazard if the valve gets sheared off in a fall — secure it upright, always. Upright also isn’t optional for a different reason: these adapters pass gaseous CO2 only. A tipped tank can send liquid CO2 into the machine, which the setup isn’t built for.

Tools/consumables: adjustable wrench, a spray bottle of soapy water for leak-checking every threaded joint, spare washers.

Where to buy

Cylinder — buy local if you can. A welding or beverage-gas supplier will sell a 5 lb aluminum cylinder and fill it on the spot with beverage-grade CO2, and you skip shipping a pressure vessel entirely. If ordering online, the VEVOR 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinder is the commonly-recommended budget option; homebrew retailers like MoreBeer and Williams Brewing carry better-vetted tanks and are reputable for this whole category.

Adapter hose:

Product Notes
Soda Helper Universal CO2 Adapter Hose (OmniFizz/Aarke Carbonator 3), 60" Low-profile hose rather than a metal-shell braided one — won’t scratch counters. Spare washers included.
Soda Helper CO2 Adapter Hose & Base Kit for OmniFizz Same hose plus a machine base — tidier countertop setup.
GURUDAR CO2 Direct Adapter, 60" stainless Listing explicitly names DrinkMate compatibility. Label warns gaseous CO2 only, tank upright.
Tiiyee CGA320 → TR21-4 with gauge and bleed valve, 60" The gauge + bleed valve combo is worth having over a bare hose.

Other reputable non-Amazon sources for the hardware in general: MoreBeer, Williams Brewing, Soda Dispenser Depot, or a local welding/gas supply shop for the tank itself.

Gas purity

An in-line filter is not the real control here, and a cheap one won’t reliably catch what actually matters: industrial and welding-grade CO2 can carry compressor oil and hydrocarbon residue that a basic filter doesn’t remove. Two things that do the real work:

  1. Specify beverage-grade / food-grade CO2 at the fill counter, every time — not the general-purpose industrial tank.
  2. Buy a new cylinder, so you’re not inheriting rust or residue from whatever the tank held in a past life.

An activated-carbon in-line gas filter from a homebrew supplier is a reasonable belt-and-suspenders addition, but largely redundant if the gas source is clean — and check its pressure rating before adding it to this unregulated, full-tank-pressure line, since most are speced for regulated low-pressure use downstream of a proper regulator.

Safety notes

  • The cylinder is the real hazard, not the gas connection. Standing, strapped, away from heat and direct sun. A cylinder is not a countertop decoration — treat it like the pressure vessel it is.
  • CO2 displaces oxygen. It’s heavier than air and pools low in a room. This is a real risk for any large-volume leak, not just a slow one — don’t store or operate the tank in a small closed cabinet with no airflow, and if you ever smell/hear a active leak, ventilate before troubleshooting.
  • Bleed the line before disconnecting. The gauge/bleed-valve hose exists specifically for this — open it to vent residual line pressure before you unscrew anything, rather than cracking a pressurized fitting open by hand.
  • Leak-test every threaded joint with soapy water after assembly — bubbles mean it’s not sealed.
  • Don’t overtighten the TR21-4 end. The washer does the sealing, not torque.
  • Drinkmate’s own warranty generally doesn’t cover damage from third-party CO2 sources — know that going in.

Before you order

  • Confirmed the machine is screw-in (TR21-4), not the push-in quick-connect used on SodaStream Terra/Art
  • Cylinder ordered/sourced: new, aluminum, CGA320, current hydro-test date, filled with beverage-grade CO2
  • Adapter hose ordered: CGA320 → TR21-4, with gauge and bleed valve if available
  • Tank strap or bracket sourced and installed before the tank goes anywhere near the counter
  • Every joint leak-tested with soapy water on first hookup
